title: The network path is dropping packets

problem.summary: Something on the network path is losing packets. Services that talk to each other over the affected path slow down and become erratic, because every lost segment has to be detected and sent again. Latency rises, but the distinguishing fact is not the latency - it is that data has to be re-sent at all. Nothing else on a healthy system does that.
symptoms: services that talk to each other are slow and erratic, while each is individually idle
latency is variable rather than uniformly higher, and gets worse for chattier callers
requests still succeed, but throughput falls
the slowdown follows a network path rather than a single component

discriminators.signal: TCP retransmission rate per interface: segments carrying a sequence number already seen on the same flow, as a share of segments
discriminators.this_problem: at least one interface retransmits heavily - measured 18.5% to 60.7% across both applications
discriminators.not_this_problem: retransmission stays low or absent. Every non-network fault measured at or below 7.1%, and most sit at exactly 0
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED across 40 labelled runs, 8 fault families, two applications. Network impairment 18.5-60.7% (one outlier at 0.15%, see unverified_do_not_claim). Slow datastore 1.2-7.1%. Co-tenant contention 0-3.9%. Cgroup cap 0-3.7%. No-fault 0-0.5%. Hung dependency and error storm exactly 0. Baseline retransmission was 0.00% in all 40 runs on both applications. See evidence/netloss_separation.json

discriminators.signal: baseline retransmission rate, as a sanity check before trusting the incident figure
discriminators.this_problem: baseline is near zero, so any retransmission during the incident is signal rather than normal behaviour
discriminators.not_this_problem: the baseline already retransmits, in which case this environment is lossy in general and the incident figure needs comparing against it rather than against zero
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED: 0.00% baseline in every one of 40 runs across both applications. This is what makes the discriminator unusually safe here - there is no noise floor to threshold against - and it is also why the check belongs in the rule rather than being assumed. See evidence/netloss_separation.json

discriminators.signal: packets queued to a device but never transmitted (net_dev_queue with no matching net_dev_xmit for the same buffer)
discriminators.this_problem: a non-zero share of buffers are dropped inside the queue. This is REQUIRED, not corroboration: it is what says the loss happened on the path rather than in a full receive buffer
discriminators.not_this_problem: every queued buffer is transmitted. A container that cannot keep up also loses packets and retransmits heavily, but it drops them in its receive buffer, so nothing is lost in the queue
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED across 84 runs on two applications: queue drops were non-zero ONLY where the impairment was applied - 0.122-0.289% and 0.055-0.125% on the first application, 0.002-0.003% on the second. Every other family measured 0.000%, with two runs at 0.001% whose retransmission was under 2.5%. See evidence/netloss_separation.json

discriminators.this_problem: reports the SCOPE of the impairment - one interface means a single service's path, many means the whole host's networking
discriminators.not_this_problem: this does not decide whether the problem is present; it describes it once the retransmission test has fired
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED and DELIBERATELY NOT a discriminator. On the first application host-wide impairment hit 7-12 interfaces against 1-3 for a single-service impairment, a clean split. On the second application the same host-wide fault hit only 0-1 interfaces against 1-2, so the split reverses and cannot be relied on. Reported as evidence of scope, never used to choose a verdict. See evidence/netloss_separation.json

unverified_do_not_claim.claim: heavy retransmission alone identifies an impaired network path
unverified_do_not_claim.status: NOT SUPPORTED - two other families retransmit as hard or harder
unverified_do_not_claim.measurement: A service memory cap retransmits 59.1-69.4% on the first application and 95.1-95.6% on the second, HARDER than any network impairment measured. Host CPU saturation crosses the same bar on two runs at 16.7% and 33.3%. Deciding on retransmission alone produced 4 false fires and 2 ambiguous verdicts across 84 runs.
unverified_do_not_claim.consequence: retransmission must be paired with queue drops. A container that cannot keep up loses packets in its receive buffer; an impaired path loses them in the queue. Only the second leaves a buffer queued and never transmitted.
unverified_do_not_claim.agent_note: How often data has to be sent again. It rises whenever packets are lost, and packets are lost for several reasons - an impaired link, but also a container too overloaded to read its socket. On its own it says packets are being lost, not where.

unverified_do_not_claim.claim: endpoint latency identifies a degraded network path
unverified_do_not_claim.measurement: Per-endpoint reply latency was measured across 40 runs. Single-service network impairment slowed 3-6 of 22 endpoints at 8.0-14.0x, overlapping healthy runs at 1-3 endpoints and 2.5-2.9x, and a slow datastore at 3-9 endpoints. On the second application it fell entirely inside the healthy range.
unverified_do_not_claim.consequence: latency changes under every fault, so it cannot be the deciding signal here. Use retransmission, which only loss produces.
unverified_do_not_claim.agent_note: How long each service endpoint takes to answer. It rises under almost every kind of fault, so on its own it says something is wrong, not what.

unverified_do_not_claim.claim: a heavily retransmitting interface is always present when the path is impaired
unverified_do_not_claim.status: PARTIALLY SUPPORTED - one run in 40 did not show it
unverified_do_not_claim.measurement: one host-wide impairment run on the second application measured 0.15% worst retransmission and 0-1 impaired interfaces, well below the 18.5% floor of every other network run. The other runs of the same family on that application reached 33.3%.
unverified_do_not_claim.consequence: this blueprint will MISS that case rather than misdiagnose it. Do not lower the threshold to capture it: the non-network ceiling is 7.1%, so doing so would trade one recovered run for false fires on slow datastores.
unverified_do_not_claim.agent_note: A path can be impaired without the trace showing much retransmission, if there is too little traffic on it during the window. Absence of retransmission is weak evidence of absence; presence is strong evidence of presence.

reproduction.system: Sock Shop or Train Ticket on Ubuntu 24.04, LTTng 2.15, Docker 27+, single GCP n2 VM
reproduction.invoke: TARGET_SVC=carts ./svc_net.sh inject aggressive   # or ./anomaly_net.sh inject aggressive
harness_only: Both recipes use tc netem inside container network namespaces on eth0, not on the host bridge - a qdisc on the bridge device does not affect L2-forwarded container-to-container frames, which was validated and recorded in the anomaly_net recipe header. svc_net impairs ONE container (aggressive: 150 ms delay, 40 ms jitter, 4% loss); anomaly_net impairs every container (aggressive: 80 ms delay, 20 ms jitter, 2% loss).

collection_order.why_these: MEASURED BASIS. net_if_receive_skb carries the full IP and TCP header, including the sequence number, so a segment repeating a sequence number already seen on its flow is a retransmission - the one effect only packet loss produces. net_dev_queue and net_dev_xmit both carry the buffer address, so a buffer queued to a device and never transmitted was dropped inside the queue, which is where the impairment sits; this corroborates. Nothing else in the kernel trace is needed, and in particular the scheduler events are irrelevant here: this fault does not change how threads are scheduled, only what happens to their packets.

processing.step: stage the stored kernel trace for reading
processing.expect: a CTF directory the trace reader can open

processing.step: count retransmissions and queue drops per interface, baseline window against incident window
processing.expect: per-interface retransmission and drop rates, and the list of impaired interfaces

processing.step: Combine into the verdict and its artifacts: the JSON verdict, the per-interface chart, and a plain-English explanation
processing.expect: name the impaired interfaces, the retransmission rate on each, and the scope

processing.step: State the recommended action alongside the diagnosis
processing.expect: map the impaired interfaces to their containers and inspect the queueing discipline and link health on that path

outputs.contains: verdict, the impaired interfaces with their retransmission rates, the baseline rate, the queue-drop rate, and the scope
retransmission rate per interface, baseline against incident
which paths are losing packets, how badly, and why that explains the slowdown better than any component being busy
map each impaired interface to its container, then check the queueing discipline, the link, and anything shaping traffic on that path

verdict_when: at least one interface retransmits 12% or more of its segments during the incident
buffers queued to that device were dropped without ever being transmitted
the same interface retransmitted at or near zero in the baseline window

rule_out.when: retransmission is high but NOTHING was dropped in the queue - the packets are being lost in a receive buffer because a container cannot keep up, not on the path
retransmission stays below a few percent while one component blocks in a socket call for an order of magnitude longer - the data is arriving intact, just late, so nothing needs re-sending
no interface retransmits meaningfully, even if endpoint latency has risen - latency alone rises under almost every fault and under ordinary load
retransmission is low and host CPU rose with a newcomer taking cores - packets are fine, the machine is busy

decision.root_cause_is: packet loss on the network path serving the impaired interfaces

evidence_from_literature.claim: Kernel-level network tracing exposes causes of request latency that distributed tracing cannot explain, because request spans record that a call was slow but not what happened to its packets
evidence_from_literature.source: Gelle, Ezzati-Jivan & Dagenais, Combining Distributed and Kernel Tracing for Performance Analysis of Cloud Applications, Electronics 10(21):2610, 2021
evidence_from_literature.validated_on: our 40-run sweep, where per-endpoint latency could not separate an impaired path from a healthy system while retransmission separated it from every other family on both applications

scenarios.note: SCENARIOS record how this problem looks on different system shapes. They are measured, not assumed, and both pictures matter: a blueprint carrying only one application's numbers would mislead anyone running the other kind of system.

cases.recognise_by: exactly one or two interfaces retransmitting, while the rest are clean
cases.what_you_see: a very high rate on the affected interface. Measured 25.6-52.6% on the first application and 38.1-60.7% on the second, with 1-3 interfaces involved.
cases.confidence: high - this was the most consistent network signature across both systems
cases.do_this_instead: map the interface to its container and inspect that container's queueing discipline first, before looking at the host network

cases.scenario: The whole host's networking is impaired
cases.what_you_see: on a short call chain, 7-12 of 16 interfaces at 18.5-40.9%. On a wide fan-out system the SAME fault reached only 0-1 interfaces, and one run showed just 0.15% - so breadth is not a reliable way to recognise this case. And on that second system the host-wide fault produced NO queue drops at all across three runs, so this blueprint misses it rather than guessing.
cases.confidence: medium on a short chain, low on a wide fan-out system
cases.do_this_instead: do not conclude host-wide impairment from interface count alone. Treat the count as evidence of scope and confirm against the actual container topology, since the same fault produced opposite breadth on the two systems we measured.

taxonomy.note: Covers any cause of packet loss on a path between services, not only injected impairment. The deciding signal is the consequence - segments being re-sent - which is the same whatever produced the loss.

apply_when: services that talk to each other are slow while each is individually idle
latency is erratic rather than uniformly raised
the slowdown follows a path rather than a component
do_not_apply_when: one component is blocked in a socket call for an order of magnitude longer while data still arrives intact
the host is short of CPU
requests are failing outright rather than slowing
applicability.cheap_precheck: count retransmissions on any one busy interface: if the rate is near zero, this blueprint does not apply and a cheaper answer exists elsewhere

capabilities_required.why: the stored kernel trace must be readable
the decisive signal: segments repeating a sequence number, which only packet loss produces
REQUIRED, not corroboration: it says the loss happened in the queue - on the path - rather than in a full receive buffer

stopping_conditions.conclude: at least one interface retransmits at 12% or more against a near-zero baseline, and queue drops corroborate
stopping_conditions.stop_and_switch: retransmission is low but one component blocks in a socket call for an order of magnitude longer -> the dependency-wait blueprint; retransmission is low and host CPU rose with a newcomer -> the CPU-contention blueprint
stopping_conditions.stop_insufficient: the network events were not recorded, so retransmission cannot be counted -> request net_if_receive_skb and re-run. Do NOT fall back to endpoint latency, which was measured not to separate this problem from a healthy system

adaptation_rules.if: the baseline window already shows meaningful retransmission
adaptation_rules.then: this environment is lossy in general. Compare the incident against that baseline rather than against zero, and lower confidence - every threshold here was measured where the baseline was exactly zero

adaptation_rules.if: retransmission is raised but only on a low-traffic interface with few segments
adaptation_rules.then: treat it as weak. A handful of segments can produce a large percentage; require enough samples before naming the path

adaptation_rules.if: no interface retransmits but the path is still suspected
adaptation_rules.then: absence is weak evidence here - one run in 40 showed an impaired path at only 0.15%. Report the negative honestly and ask for traffic-level evidence on the specific path rather than concluding it is healthy

preconditions: kernel network events are collectable or already collected
traffic on the suspected path is heavy enough to sample

historical_effectiveness.note: 12 labelled network runs across two applications, scored against 72 runs of ten other families. 9 of 12 correct with no false fires; the 3 misses are all the host-wide fault on the second application, which produces neither queue drops nor reliable retransmission there.

policies.collection_order_rule: Use evidence that already exists before enabling any new collection. Escalate a tier only when the cheaper tier leaves a candidate cause unresolved, and record why.

scope.restrict_to: the hosts and time window named in the intent

privacy: record only packet headers, never packet contents
do not retain personally identifiable data

requires_approval: widening the host scope or time window

policies.autonomy_note: Level 2 = policy-controlled automation: select and execute low-risk plans inside the stated constraints.

evidence_sufficiency.if_below_floor: name the unresolved question, pick the ONE additional capability that would settle it, check it against the overhead budget, and request it.
evidence_sufficiency.report_when_stuck: if the floor is still not met after the allowed rounds, report the best-supported hypothesis, its confidence, and precisely what evidence is missing - never present a guess as a diagnosis

provenance.authored_by: measured from the packet-loss sweep, 40 labelled runs across 8 families and two applications
provenance.notes: Written after per-endpoint LATENCY failed to separate this fault from a healthy system on either application (finding F13). The turn came from asking what is mechanically specific to a network fault: it is the only family in the catalogue that drops packets, and a dropped segment must be re-sent. Deliberately ONE blueprint rather than two: breadth separates host-wide from single-service impairment on the first application (7-12 interfaces against 1-3) and reverses on the second (0-1 against 1-2), so splitting them would assert a distinction that only holds on one system. Scope is reported as evidence instead. v2 (2026-08-31): queue drops promoted from corroboration to a required test after finding F17. Retransmission alone was measured NOT to be specific - a service memory cap retransmits harder than any network fault, because an overloaded container drops packets in its receive buffer. The first sweep had covered 8 of 13 families and missed that one, which is precisely the check the specificity protocol exists to force. v3: fault_type set to the ground-truth FAMILY name (anomaly_net). This field becomes `covers:` in the generated skill, which the harness matches against the family, and the diagnosis scorer falls back to identity for unknown labels - so a family name satisfies both, while the agent's own fault vocabulary satisfies only the second.
